newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banks to face increased competition - survey.
newsitem.headline: German banks to face increased competition - survey.

text.p: The globalisation of international financial markets poses competitive challenges to German banks, especially when currency union becomes a reality, leading German bankers said on Tuesday in a newspaper survey.

The introduction of the Euro will make European financial markets more attractive to institutional investors from the U.S. and Japan, said Hilmar Kopper, outgoing chief executive of Deutsche Bank in a survey in Germany's Boersen-Zeitung.
As competition increased, there would be further consolidation and cost-cutting in the banking sector, and not only in Germany, Kopper said.
"We have to identify and exploit areas where savings can be made and synergies introduced," said Kopper.
"Attempts by foreign banks to win worthwhile market share in Germany have not been very successful to date. That could change more quickly than expected,"

"The introduction of the Euro in 1999 will accelerate this process as the disappearance of the deutschemark also signals the end of one of the most important competitive strengths enjoyed by German banks," said Kopper.
"Without competition we would probably sleep better, but live worse," said Kopper, who retires as CEO of Deutsche in May.

Chief executive of Dresdner Bank, Juergen Sarrazin, also said in the survey that German banks are well-positioned to cope with the competitive pressures from increased globalisation and by currency union in 1997.

"The big German banks, with their different earnings centres, are well-equipped to take advantage of the opportunities offered at home and abroad by the changes in the financial markets," said Sarrazin.

Sarrazin said Dresdner, Germany's second-largest bank, was basing its reaction to competitive changes on four strategic areas -- private banking, corporate banking, investment banking and asset management.
The trend in private banking was towards higher levels of service and customer advice, while services like telebanking and direct banking would continue to grow, said Sarrazin.
New developments in financial instruments and technology would lead to corporate customers being offered a more complex palette of products.
"Investment banking will take on more importance with a view to cross-border acquisitions and takeovers and the expected increase in the number of privatisations," said Sarrazin.
The growth in funds worldwide and the increased necessity for private pension provision meant there was great potential in the asset management area, Sarrazin said.

Martin Kohlhaussen, chief executive of Germany's third largest bank, Commerzbank AG, said that underperforming branches in Germany's banking sector will face closure or consolidation from next year onwards.
"The domestic branch system is facing a crucial test," Kohlhaussen said.
"Clearly nobody is considering withdrawing from the area, but on cost-utility grounds, unprofitable branches will face consolidation or closure," he added.

Commerzbank in November launched a major questionnaire among its customers in a move seen as part of a cultural move by German banks to become more efficient and reassess their cost-laden branch networks.
